items.question: How would you design a database transaction for related writes?
items.answer: I would make the related writes part of one transaction so they commit atomically or roll back together. I would choose the isolation level based on consistency needs, keep the transaction short, and add indexes for the access pattern while checking their write cost.

items.question: Explain the time complexity of binary search and when it applies.
items.answer: Binary search repeatedly halves a sorted search space, so it takes O(log n) time and O(1) extra space in an iterative implementation. It requires an ordered, randomly accessible collection; otherwise a linear scan or another index may be more appropriate.

items.question: How would you design a REST API for updating a user profile?
items.answer: I would expose an endpoint for the profile and validate the request. The API should return a useful status code and store the changes. I would also add authentication and tests.

items.question: What are the main trade-offs of adding a database index?
items.answer: An index can make reads faster because the database does not need to scan every row. It takes extra storage and can make inserts and updates slower. I would add indexes based on real query patterns.

items.question: How do you prevent a deadlock between concurrent operations?
items.answer: I would use locks carefully and try to avoid deadlocks.

items.question: What makes an HTTP API reliable in production?
items.answer: It should handle errors and have monitoring.

items.question: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
items.answer: A thread is a completely separate program with its own memory, while a process is just a lightweight part of a thread. Threads cannot share memory, so they are always isolated from each other.

items.question: Why are database transactions useful?
items.answer: Transactions mainly compress database tables and automatically make every query run in constant time. They are only needed for read-only queries and cannot roll back changes.
